claim: Heritability of human lifespan is 23–33% as evident from twin studies.
source: Heritability of human lifespan is 23–33% as evident from twin studies.
evidence: Supported by citation to twin studies

claim: The burden of rarest protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in two large cohorts is negatively associated with human healthspan and lifespan, accounting for 0.4 and 1.3 years of their variability, respectively.
source: Here, we report that the burden of rarest protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in two large cohorts is negatively associated with human healthspan and lifespan, accounting for 0.4 and 1.3 years of their variability, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data from analysis of two cohorts (UKB and UKBBN)

claim: Longer-living individuals possess both fewer rarest PTVs and less damaging PTVs.
source: In addition, longer-living individuals possess both fewer rarest PTVs and less damaging PTVs.
evidence: Supported by data analysis comparing PTV burden and characteristics across individuals with different lifespans

claim: Somatic accumulation of PTVs accounts for only a small fraction of mortality and morbidity acceleration and hence is unlikely to be causal in aging.
source: We further estimated that somatic accumulation of PTVs accounts for only a small fraction of mortality and morbidity acceleration and hence is unlikely to be causal in aging.
evidence: Based on inference from calculations comparing somatic PTV accumulation rates to observed mortality acceleration

claim: Rare damaging mutations, both inherited and accumulated throughout life, contribute to the aging process.
source: We conclude that rare damaging mutations, both inherited and accumulated throughout life, contribute to the aging process, and that burden of ultra-rare variants in combination with common alleles better explain apparent heritability of human lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data analysis of germline and somatic mutations

claim: Burden of ultra-rare variants in combination with common alleles better explain apparent heritability of human lifespan.
source: We conclude that rare damaging mutations, both inherited and accumulated throughout life, contribute to the aging process, and that burden of ultra-rare variants in combination with common alleles better explain apparent heritability of human lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from data analysis and comparison with previous GWAS findings

claim: GWAS on centenarians consistently demonstrate loci near APOE gene to be associated with extreme longevity.
source: For example, GWAS on centenarians consistently demonstrate loci near APOE gene to be associated with extreme longevity, and loci near FOXO3A, HLA-DQA1 and SH2B3 genes to have population-specific associations (Melzer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melzer et al., 2020

claim: Loci near FOXO3A, HLA-DQA1 and SH2B3 genes have population-specific associations with extreme longevity.
source: For example, GWAS on centenarians consistently demonstrate loci near APOE gene to be associated with extreme longevity, and loci near FOXO3A, HLA-DQA1 and SH2B3 genes to have population-specific associations (Melzer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melzer et al., 2020

claim: Centenarians represent less than 0.1% of the population in developed countries.
source: However, even in developed countries, centenarians represent less than 0.1% of the population, and the genetic determinants responsible for the survival of general population remain poorly understood.
evidence: Based on established demographic knowledge

claim: The combined contribution of common variants could explain only a small fraction of the lifespan variation.
source: However, the combined contribution of common variants could explain only a small fraction of the lifespan variation as most of the individuals lack any of the alleles previously associated with lifespan.
evidence: Based on inference from previous GWAS studies and citation to prior work

claim: Ultra-rare variants are enriched for damaging alleles.
source: These ultra-rare variants, most notably protein-truncating variants (PTVs), are known to be enriched for damaging alleles.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: An inverse relationship between variant's minor allele frequency (MAF) and effect size was recently demonstrated for type II diabetes.
source: An inverse relationship between variant's minor allele frequency (MAF) and effect size was recently demonstrated for type II diabetes, an archetypal age-related disease (Mahajan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahajan et al., 2018

claim: Multi-tissue gene expression outliers were enriched with rare variants in the GTEx dataset.
source: Multi-tissue gene expression outliers were enriched with rare variants in the GTEx dataset (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2017

claim: Most of the underexpressed outliers harbor rare PTVs, which are more likely to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) than common variants.
source: Most of the underexpressed outliers harbor rare PTVs, which are more likely to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) than common variants (Rivas et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rivas et al., 2015

claim: Nonsense variants with a high Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion score were enriched in singletons.
source: Additionally, ExAC consortium demonstrated that the nonsense variants with a high Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion score (Rentzsch et al., 2019), a widely used predictor of deleteriousness of single-nucleotide variants, were enriched in singletons (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lek et al., 2016

claim: PTVs are substantially enriched for deleterious alleles.
source: Although missense and non-coding variants may also be damaging, PTVs are substantially enriched for deleterious alleles.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: PTVs alter gene expression more dramatically than missense and untranslated region (UTR) variants.
source: They also alter gene expression more dramatically than missense and untranslated region (UTR) variants (GTEx Consortium et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to GTEx Consortium et al., 2017

claim: Ultra-rare PTVs are usually eliminated by purifying selection.
source: Ultra-rare PTVs are usually eliminated by purifying selection, but the small effective population size of humans means that they are present in all human genomes.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary genetics knowledge

claim: The small effective population size of humans means that ultra-rare PTVs are present in all human genomes.
source: Ultra-rare PTVs are usually eliminated by purifying selection, but the small effective population size of humans means that they are present in all human genomes.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary genetics knowledge

claim: Increased rare PTV burden was associated with complex diseases, such as schizophrenia, epilepsy and autism.
source: Increased rare PTV burden was associated with complex diseases, such as schizophrenia, epilepsy and autism (Leu et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2016), whereas individual genetic variants exhibited small effects.
evidence: Supported by citations to Leu et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2016

claim: The burden of rare PTVs in genes intolerant to such variants was negatively associated with years of schooling (academic attainment).
source: This analysis revealed a negative association with years of schooling (academic attainment) and a positive association with intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (Ganna et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganna et al., 2018

claim: The burden of rare PTVs in genes intolerant to such variants was positively associated with intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
source: This analysis revealed a negative association with years of schooling (academic attainment) and a positive association with intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (Ganna et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganna et al., 2018

claim: The age at enrollment was negatively correlated with the burden of PI-PTVs, suggesting a possible association with lifespan.
source: Notably, the age at enrollment was also negatively correlated with the burden of PI-PTVs, suggesting a possible association with lifespan.
evidence: Based on inference from data reported by Ganna et al., 2018

claim: The UKB cohort included 40,368 individuals who self-reported 'White British' and were of close genetic ancestry.
source: We selected a cohort of 40,368 individuals from UKB with sequenced exomes who self-reported 'White British' and were of close genetic ancestry based on a principal component analysis of their genotypes (Bycroft et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of study cohort

claim: Of the UKB cohort, 21,742 (54%) were males with mean age of 58.1 years (SD = 7.9, age range 40.2 − 70.6).
source: Of those, 21,742 (54%) were males with mean age of 58.1 years (SD = 7.9, age range 40.2 − 70.6) and 18,626 (46%) were females with mean age of 57 years (SD = 7.8, age range 40.1 − 70.4) at the time of assessment.
evidence: Description of study cohort demographics

claim: Of the UKB cohort, 18,626 (46%) were females with mean age of 57 years (SD = 7.8, age range 40.1 − 70.4) at the time of assessment.
source: Of those, 21,742 (54%) were males with mean age of 58.1 years (SD = 7.9, age range 40.2 − 70.6) and 18,626 (46%) were females with mean age of 57 years (SD = 7.8, age range 40.1 − 70.4) at the time of assessment.
evidence: Description of study cohort demographics

claim: In the UKB cohort, 1,122 subjects died during the follow-up period of 11 years (2005 − 2016), mostly of cancer.
source: In the UKB cohort, 1,122 subjects died during the follow-up period of 11 years (2005 − 2016), mostly of cancer (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2 showing causes of death

claim: The UKBBN cohort included 1,105 deceased subjects of European origin after excluding cases of suicides, accidents, and cases of death with no abnormalities detected.
source: The UKBBN cohort included 1,105 deceased subjects of European origin after we excluded cases of suicides, accidents, and cases of death with no abnormalities detected.
evidence: Description of study cohort

claim: Of the UKBBN cohort, 489 (44%) were females with mean age of 71.2 years (SD = 18, age range 16 − 103 years).
source: Of those, 489 (44%) were females with mean age of 71.2 years (SD = 18, age range 16 − 103 years) and 616 (56%) were males with mean age of 67.7 years (SD = 17, age range 17 − 105 years).
evidence: Description of study cohort demographics

claim: Of the UKBBN cohort, 616 (56%) were males with mean age of 67.7 years (SD = 17, age range 17 − 105 years).
source: Of those, 489 (44%) were females with mean age of 71.2 years (SD = 18, age range 16 − 103 years) and 616 (56%) were males with mean age of 67.7 years (SD = 17, age range 17 − 105 years).
evidence: Description of study cohort demographics

claim: Most participants in the UKBBN study were diagnosed with neurodegenerative diseases, for example Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Pick's diseases.
source: Most participants in this study were diagnosed with neurodegenerative diseases, for example Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Pick's diseases (Keogh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Keogh et al., 2017

claim: The Cox regression coefficients were very similar in UKBBN and UKB datasets, indicating consistency of the effect across populations.
source: Moreover, the Cox regression coefficients were very similar in UKBBN and UKB datasets, indicating consistency of the effect across populations despite differences in population structure and morbidity statistics (Table 2), tissue source (blood in UKB and brain in UKBBN), sequencing methods and variant calling pipelines (Keogh et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison of Cox regression results between two cohorts

claim: A smaller but still significant effect of the ultra-rare PTV burden was observed on mothers' but not on fathers' age at death in UKB.
source: We also observed a smaller but still significant effect of the ultra-rare PTV burden on mothers' but not on fathers' age at death in UKB.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis

claim: The effect size on mother's age at death was smaller and less significant than that on the subject's healthspan and lifespan.
source: The effect size on mother's age at death was smaller and less significant than that on the subject's healthspan and lifespan.
evidence: Based on comparison of Cox regression coefficients

claim: Association with age at death was similar between the sexes.
source: Association with age at death was similar between the sexes.
evidence: Supported by sex-stratified analysis shown in Table 3

claim: The associations with healthspan and mother's age at death were almost entirely driven by women.
source: However, the associations with healthspan and mother's age at death were almost entirely driven by women.
evidence: Supported by sex-stratified analysis shown in Table 3

claim: Only stop gains were associated with mother's age at death among PTV types.
source: However, only stop gains were associated with mother's age at death, and none of the categories were associated with father's age at death.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: None of the PTV categories were associated with father's age at death.
source: However, only stop gains were associated with mother's age at death, and none of the categories were associated with father's age at death.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Synonymous variants showed no significant associations with lifespan phenotypes.
source: As a negative control, we also included the effects of neutral variants - synonymous variants, which showed no significant associations with lifespan phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis

claim: Ultra-rare PTVs affect 89% of the sequenced genes in the UKB dataset.
source: Ultra-rare PTVs affect 89% of the sequenced genes in the UKB dataset.
evidence: Based on analysis of variant distribution across genes

claim: 11% of sequenced genes in the UKB dataset had no ultra-rare PTVs observed, referred to as genes intolerant to rare PTVs (iPTV).
source: No ultra-rare PTVs were observed in the remaining 11%, which we refer as genes intolerant to rare PTVs (iPTV).
evidence: Based on analysis of variant distribution across genes

claim: iPTV genes, on average, were expressed in a higher number of tissues.
source: iPTV genes, on average, were expressed in a higher number of tissues (Figure 4a) and had higher indispensability scores (a metric to measure gene essentiality introduced by Khurana et al., 2013; Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a

claim: iPTV genes had higher indispensability scores.
source: iPTV genes, on average, were expressed in a higher number of tissues (Figure 4a) and had higher indispensability scores (a metric to measure gene essentiality introduced by Khurana et al., 2013; Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b

claim: iPTV genes in the UKB cohort are strongly enriched in genes intolerant to PTVs measured by pLI scores.
source: As expected, iPTV genes in the UKB cohort are strongly enriched in genes intolerant to PTVs measured by pLI scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), confirming that genes intolerant to PTVs largely overlap between UKB and ExAC datasets.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: Genes intolerant to PTVs largely overlap between UKB and ExAC datasets.
source: As expected, iPTV genes in the UKB cohort are strongly enriched in genes intolerant to PTVs measured by pLI scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), confirming that genes intolerant to PTVs largely overlap between UKB and ExAC datasets.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of pLI scores between datasets

claim: Genes that harbored frequent PTVs had tissue-specific expressions and had lower indispensability scores.
source: Accordingly, genes that harbored frequent PTVs had tissue-specific expressions and had lower indispensability scores, thus were less essential, in agreement with previously published results for ExAC cohort (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to Lek et al., 2016

claim: Ultra-rare stop gains were more likely to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) as predicted by snpEff by 50 base-pair rule.
source: Ultra-rare stop gains were more likely to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (Figure 4c) as predicted by snpEff by 50 base-pair rule (Maquat, 2004) which was also demonstrated for the rare variants in GTEx dataset (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4c and citations

claim: Subjects dying earlier harbored more damaging PTVs.
source: Our analysis confirmed the idea that subjects dying younger harbored more damaging PTVs.
evidence: Supported by analysis comparing gene characteristics between subjects with different lifespans

claim: PTVs in shorter-lived subjects affect more broadly expressed genes.
source: Those variants affect more broadly expressed genes, based on GTEx gene expression data (Figure 5c), and cause gene loss-of-function more frequently (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5c

claim: PTVs in shorter-lived subjects cause gene loss-of-function more frequently.
source: Those variants affect more broadly expressed genes, based on GTEx gene expression data (Figure 5c), and cause gene loss-of-function more frequently (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5e

claim: PTVs in shorter-lived subjects resided in genes less likely to maintain a wild-type phenotype when a single copy of the gene is inactivated, as evident by genome-wide haploinsufficiency score GHIS.
source: PTVs in shorter-lived subjects also resided in genes less likely to maintain a wild-type phenotype when a single copy of the gene is inactivated, as evident by genome-wide haploinsufficiency score GHIS from Steinberg et al. (2015); Figure 5b.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5b and citation to Steinberg et al. (2015)

claim: PTVs in shorter-lived subjects affected genes with stronger constraints against PTVs, based on the observed/expected LoF (oe, gnomAD v2.1) scores.
source: Also, these PTVs affected genes with stronger constraints against PTVs, based on the observed/expected LoF (oe, gnomAD v2.1) scores, suggesting that these genes harbored fewer PTVs than expected in the general population.
evidence: Supported by analysis of oe scores shown in Figure 5d

claim: Percent of tissues expressing genes, oe scores and loss-of-function occurrence were all significantly associated with lifespan of subjects with 5 PTVs.
source: Percent of tissues expressing these genes, oe scores and loss-of-function occurrence were all significantly associated with lifespan of subjects with 5 PTVs (Figure 5a, inset).
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis shown in Figure 5a inset

claim: None of the genes reached statistical significance under FDR p-value cut-off of 0.05 in gene burden test for lifespan or healthspan.
source: Interestingly, none of the genes reached statistical significance under FDR p-value cut-off of 0.05 (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test for gene burden analysis

claim: 110 genes were prone to ultra-rare PTVs in the UKB cohort.
source: By comparing the number of PTVs and synonymous variants per gene, to the overall number of those variants, we found 110 genes that were prone to ultra-rare PTVs, as well as 188 genes intolerant to those variants (Supplementary file 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test comparing PTVs and synonymous variants

claim: 188 genes were intolerant to ultra-rare PTVs in the UKB cohort.
source: By comparing the number of PTVs and synonymous variants per gene, to the overall number of those variants, we found 110 genes that were prone to ultra-rare PTVs, as well as 188 genes intolerant to those variants (Supplementary file 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on Fisher's exact test comparing PTVs and synonymous variants

claim: Genes prone to ultra-rare PTVs in UKB showed high oe scores in gnomAD.
source: Our estimations were in agreement with oe scores provided by gnomAD. As expected, genes prone to ultra-rare PTVs in UKB showed high oe scores in gnomAD, while genes intolerant to those variants had low oe scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison with gnomAD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Genes intolerant to ultra-rare PTVs in UKB had low oe scores in gnomAD.
source: Our estimations were in agreement with oe scores provided by gnomAD. As expected, genes prone to ultra-rare PTVs in UKB showed high oe scores in gnomAD, while genes intolerant to those variants had low oe scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison with gnomAD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: The estimated effect of somatic PTV accumulation is minor in comparison to the effect of germline PTV burden.
source: The estimated effect of somatic PTV accumulation is minor in comparison to the effect of germline PTV burden, and can account only for a minute fraction of mortality and morbidity acceleration.
evidence: Based on comparison of calculated somatic and germline PTV effects

claim: Somatic PTV accumulation can account only for a minute fraction of mortality and morbidity acceleration.
source: The estimated effect of somatic PTV accumulation is minor in comparison to the effect of germline PTV burden, and can account only for a minute fraction of mortality and morbidity acceleration.
evidence: Based on calculation comparing somatic mutation accumulation to Gompertz mortality acceleration

claim: Both lifespan and healthspan are negatively impacted by the burden of rarest variants that disrupt genes and are already present at birth.
source: We report that both lifespan and healthspan are negatively impacted by the burden of rarest variants that disrupt genes and are already present at birth.
evidence: Conclusion based on Cox proportional hazards analysis of germline PTVs

claim: The genetic component of lifespan is shaped by two mutation types: common variants and ultra-rare PTVs.
source: In this regard, we find that the genetic component of lifespan is shaped by two mutation types: common variants, as found by previous studies, and ultra-rare PTVs, as shown here.
evidence: Conclusion based on integration of current findings with previous GWAS studies

claim: The association of ultra-rare PTV mutations with healthspan reflects the effect of deleterious gene variants on the incidence of the first chronic disease.
source: The association of ultra-rare PTV mutations with healthspan, however, reflects the effect of deleterious gene variants on the incidence of the first chronic disease and thus covers the accumulated effect of genotype on health and survival over a much longer time, effectively from birth up to the age of enrollment/death.
evidence: Based on interpretation of healthspan definition and analysis results

claim: The association of ultra-rare mutation burden and lifespan is consistent between the UKB and UKBBN cohorts.
source: The association of ultra-rare mutation burden and lifespan is consistent between the UKB and UKBBN cohorts.
evidence: Based on comparison of Cox regression results between cohorts

claim: UKB subjects exhibit lower mortality and hence are probably healthier than the general population.
source: On the other hand, UKB subjects exhibit lower mortality and hence are probably healthier than the general population (Ganna and Ingelsson, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganna and Ingelsson, 2015

claim: The association of ultra-rare mutations and lifespan traits is a general feature that applies to the UK population.
source: It, therefore, appears that the association of ultra-rare mutations and lifespan traits is a general feature that applies to the UK population.
evidence: Inferred from consistency of results across UKB and UKBBN cohorts

claim: There is an open question whether the findings are translatable to the populations outside UK and Europe.
source: However, there is still an open question whether our findings are translatable to the populations outside UK and Europe.
evidence: Speculation about generalizability of findings

claim: A genetic correlation between longevity and father's age at death was reported to be one of the strongest.
source: At the same time, a genetic correlation between longevity and father's age at death was reported to be one of the strongest (Deelen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deelen et al., 2019

claim: Ultra-rare PTV burden may be more relevant for lifespan than for longevity.
source: One of explanations would be that ultra-rare PTV burden is more relevant for lifespan than for longevity.
evidence: Speculation to explain lack of association with father's age at death

claim: Men had a much shorter healthspan compared to women (Cox ph beta = 0.16, p-value=1.55E-18).
source: At the same time, men had a much shorter healthspan compared to women (Cox ph beta = 0.16, p-value=1.55E-18).
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis

claim: The genetic component, represented by ultra-rare PTVs, may play a less important role in male healthspan due to lifestyle choices such as smoking, drinking, risky behavior and unhealthy diet.
source: We hypothesize that the genetic component, represented here by ultra-rare PTVs, may play a less important role in male healthspan due to the lifestyle choices such as smoking, drinking, risky behavior and unhealthy diet.
evidence: Hypothesis to explain sex-specific effects

claim: Men smoke more than women in UKB.
source: Indeed, men are known to smoke more (Peters et al., 2014), drink more, and exhibit higher BMI scores (Wills et al., 2017) than women in UKB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Peters et al., 2014

claim: Men drink more and exhibit higher BMI scores than women in UKB.
source: Indeed, men are known to smoke more (Peters et al., 2014), drink more, and exhibit higher BMI scores (Wills et al., 2017) than women in UKB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wills et al., 2017

claim: No associations of X-chromosome PTV burden with either lifespan or healthspan were found in men.
source: We found no associations of X-chromosome PTV burden with either lifespan or healthspan.
evidence: Based on Cox proportional hazards analysis of X-chromosome PTVs

claim: The number of PTVs per individual specifically on X chromosome is extremely low.
source: However, the number of PTVs per individual specifically on X chromosome is extremely low; thus, we may be out of power to pick up the difference.
evidence: Based on observation of variant counts

claim: 1,496 genes are free of ultra-rare PTVs in the whole UKB population sequenced so far.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a subset of 1,496 genes that are free of ultra-rare PTVs in the whole UKB population sequenced so far.
evidence: Based on analysis of variant distribution across genes

claim: Genes free of ultra-rare PTVs are more essential as evidenced by high indispensability scores and are expressed more broadly throughout the body.
source: These genes are more essential as evidenced by high indispensability scores and are expressed more broadly throughout the body.
evidence: Based on analysis of gene characteristics

claim: Disruption of genes free of ultra-rare PTVs could lead to either childhood or embryonic lethality.
source: Their disruption could lead to either childhood or embryonic lethality, the time periods that are not covered by UKB as well as other public datasets, for example ExAC.
evidence: Inference based on gene essentiality and absence of PTVs

claim: Common PTVs are expected to have a lower effect on fitness than ultra-rare PTVs.
source: Overall, common PTVs are expected to have a lower effect on fitness, which would explain the lack of the association between the burden of common PTVs and lifespan phenotypes.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary principles and gene characteristics

claim: Ultra-rare PTVs are more damaging than common PTVs but not enough damaging to cause early life mortality.
source: It is apparent that the ultra-rare PTVs are more damaging than common PTVs but not enough damaging to cause early life mortality.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of variant characteristics and association results

claim: The discrepancy in lifespan among individuals sharing same PTV number might be explained by differences in the rate of age-related damage accumulation, regulated by environment and genetic factors.
source: This discrepancy might be explained by differences in the rate of age-related damage accumulation, regulated by environment and genetic factors.
evidence: Speculation about factors contributing to lifespan variability

claim: The impact of a PTV on phenotype depends on the gene it disrupts and its position within the gene body.
source: In addition, the impact of a PTV on phenotype depends on the gene it disrupts and its position within the gene body.
evidence: Based on established genetic knowledge

claim: Both the degree of damage caused by ultra-rare PTVs and the number of these variants are important factors influencing human lifespan.
source: Thus, both the degree of damage caused by ultra-rare PTVs and the number of these variants are important factors influencing human lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion based on analysis of PTV characteristics and lifespan associations

claim: The effect size of ultra-rare PTVs on lifespan was comparable to the effect of known longevity alleles.
source: Intriguingly, the effect size of ultra-rare PTVs on lifespan was comparable to the effect of known longevity alleles.
evidence: Based on comparison of effect sizes

claim: There is little evidence for a significant role of somatic mutations in aging.
source: Thus, we found little evidence for a significant role of somatic mutations in aging (Promislow and Tatar, 1998; Moorad and Promislow, 2008).
evidence: Conclusion based on calculation of somatic mutation effects

claim: Somatic mutations may play a role through high-order effects, such as clonal expansion and cell competition, and hence amplify the effects of other forms of damage.
source: Somatic mutations may, however, play a role through high-order effects, such as clonal expansion and cell competition, and hence amplify the effects of other forms of damage (Martincorena, 2019).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Martincorena, 2019

claim: The effects of common variants earlier implicated in longevity and the effects of ultra-rare variants could help explain the apparent heritability of lifespan.
source: Taken together, the effects of common variants earlier implicated in longevity and the effects of ultra-rare variants reported here could help explain the apparent heritability of lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion based on integration of current findings with previous studies

claim: A more recent study puts up a challenge to the 23-33% heritability conclusion and points to a much lower level of genetic determinism.
source: A more recent study (Ruby et al., 2018) puts up a challenge to this conclusion and points to a much lower level of genetic determinism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruby et al., 2018

claim: Future investigations of the effects of ultra-rare genetic variants may turn to be crucial for quantitative understanding of lifespan heritability.
source: We therefore expect that future investigations of the effects of ultra-rare genetic variants may turn to be crucial for quantitative understanding of lifespan heritability.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions

claim: Aging is a systemic process resulting from the combined accumulation of age-related deleterious changes, none of which could cause aging on their own.
source: These findings strengthen the case for complexity of aging, wherein aging is a systemic process resulting from the combined accumulation of age-related deleterious changes, none of which could cause aging on their own (Gladyshev, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gladyshev, 2016

claim: The advantage of mutations in aging studies is that they can be quantified and their contribution estimated.
source: The advantage of mutations in aging studies, however, is that they can be quantified and their contribution estimated, which is something that is currently much more difficult to do for other forms of age-related damage.
evidence: Based on comparison of measurability of different types of age-related damage

claim: The first batch of UKB exome sequence group consists of 49,960 individuals who passed QC procedures by UKB.
source: The first batch of UKB exome sequence group consists of 49,960 individuals who passed QC procedures by UKB.
evidence: Description of data source

claim: The exome sequencing cohort is enriched with samples with a higher rate of imaging and enhanced measurements.
source: Exome sequencing cohort is enriched with samples with a higher rate of imaging and enhanced measurements such as retinal optical coherence tomography test, visual acuity, hearing test, and other.
evidence: Description of cohort characteristics

claim: The exome sequencing cohort is not biased on any health condition, disease or physical measurement results from the UKB population.
source: This cohort is not biased on any health condition, disease or physical measurement results from the UKB population of almost 500,000 individuals (Hout et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hout et al., 2019

claim: The Cox regression coefficient for males was 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.59) in UKB.
source: The Cox regression coefficients for males were 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.59) in UKB and 0.26 (95% CI 0.13–0.38) in UKBBN.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis

claim: The Cox regression coefficient for males was 0.26 (95% CI 0.13–0.38) in UKBBN.
source: The Cox regression coefficients for males were 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.59) in UKB and 0.26 (95% CI 0.13–0.38) in UKBBN.
evidence: Supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis

claim: Under constant mortality acceleration, the Cox regression coefficient for males would correspond to approximately 3 − 5 years of difference in life expectancy.
source: Under constant mortality acceleration, this would correspond to approximately 3 − 5 years of difference in life expectancy.
evidence: Calculated from Cox regression coefficients

claim: Women in the UK live longer than men, although the gap between the sexes has decreased over time down to 3.7 years.
source: Women in the UK (the population relevant to this study) live longer than men, although the gap between the sexes has decreased over time down to 3.7 years (Sanders, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanders, 2017

claim: The incidence of major chronic diseases in UKB increases exponentially with age in accordance to Gompertz law.
source: In Zenin et al. (2019), we observed that the incidence of major chronic diseases (such as Congestive Heart Failure (CHF), Myocardial Infarction (MI), Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), stroke, dementia, diabetes, cancer, and death) in UKB increases exponentially with age in accordance to Gompertz law.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zenin et al., 2019

claim: 28% of UKB participants were diagnosed with at least one of the selected diseases by the time of the first assessment.
source: As much as 28% of UKB participants were diagnosed with at least one of the selected diseases by the time of the first assessment.
evidence: Based on analysis of UKB health records

claim: Exome data consisted of 8,959,608 SNPs and short indels from human coding DNA.
source: Exome data consisted of 8,959,608 SNPs and short indels from human coding DNA.
evidence: Description of data

claim: 152,790 and 11,393 SNPs and indels were identified as PTVs in UKB and UKBBN, respectively.
source: In downstream analysis we focused on protein-truncating variants annotated as: stop codon gained, frameshift variant, slice donor or splice acceptor site, this produced 152,790 and 11,393 SNPs and indels in UKB and UKBBN, correspondingly.
evidence: Description of variant annotation results

claim: Mortality in the UKB dataset reflects the progression rate of age-related chronic diseases in an individual.
source: However, due to the limited follow-up, mortality in the UKB dataset reflects the progression rate of age-related chronic diseases in an individual; that is if a subject is deceased, he/she most probably had one or more age-related disease at the time of enrollment.
evidence: Inference based on follow-up period and disease prevalence

claim: UKB subjects included in lifespan analysis are biased toward shorter lifespan.
source: As a result, UKB subjects included in lifespan analysis are biased toward shorter lifespan.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with general UK population

claim: A general UK population born at the same time as UKB subjects had a life expectancy at birth of 71 years.
source: A general UK population born at the same time had a life expectancy at birth of 71 years which is much longer compared to the average lifespan of 57 years in the deceased UKB cohort.
evidence: Based on demographic data

claim: UKBBN subjects had an average lifespan of 69 years.
source: On the other hand, UKBBN subjects had an average lifespan of 69 years which is closer to the actual lifespan in the UK.
evidence: Based on analysis of UKBBN cohort

claim: UKBBN subjects were born in the period spanning the whole century from 1891 to 1996.
source: However, subjects in the UKBBN cohort were born in the period spanning the whole century from 1891 to 1996.
evidence: Description of cohort characteristics

claim: Deleterious alleles might accumulate in recent generations due to advances in medicine.
source: As one would expect, deleterious alleles might accumulate in recent generations due to advances in medicine.
evidence: Based on evolutionary reasoning

claim: The UKBBN cohort may be enriched for individuals prone to diseases and death at any given age.
source: By the nature of its design, the UKBBN cohort may be enriched for individuals prone to diseases and death at any given age.
evidence: Inference based on cohort design (brain bank)
